explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think so. A man with this much to carry might keep somebody close for the night. But the text says Jacob sent his family across the stream, along with all his possessions (Genesis 32:23). Then it says, “So Jacob was left all alone…” (Genesis 32:24). Nobody stayed, not even one servant.

Right, and it's a lonely picture. Jacob sent his family and all his possessions across the stream (Genesis 32:23). The text then says, “So Jacob was left all alone…” (Genesis 32:24). No servants, no helpers. Just Jacob, the dark, and whoever shows up next.

explanations.answer: He strikes the socket of Jacob's hip
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. When the man saw he could not overpower Jacob, he struck the socket of Jacob's hip and dislocated it as they wrestled (Genesis 32:25). One touch, and the whole fight changes. I'd have tapped out right there.

explanations.answer: He shoves Jacob into the stream
explanations.explanation: The stream is where Jacob sent his family across, but nobody gets shoved into it. The text says the man struck the socket of Jacob's hip and dislocated it (Genesis 32:25). That's the move, and it hurts a lot more than a splash.

explanations.answer: He lets go and slips off into the dark
explanations.explanation: Nope, nobody is slipping off yet. The man asks Jacob to let him go, so he's still being held (Genesis 32:26). What he does when he can't overpower Jacob is strike the socket of his hip (Genesis 32:25). The wrestling keeps right on going.

Yes, Israel. The man says, “Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel…” (Genesis 32:28). That's a name the whole nation will carry later, which is a big thing to get from one long night. I think Jacob walked in with one name and walked out with a brand new one.

Abraham is a good guess, since he was Jacob's grandfather. Isaac, Jacob's father, was Abraham's son (Genesis 25:19). But the man gives Jacob a different name, “Israel” (Genesis 32:28). Abraham's name stays with Abraham.

Joshua doesn't come up in this passage at all. The man says, “Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel…” (Genesis 32:28). That's the name Jacob walks away with. Good thing to know before the next stop.

That's the word, baker. The man says, “…because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed.” (Genesis 32:28). Jacob walks off limping and still gets called a winner. That's a strange kind of win, and I love it.

Fled is a fair guess, because Jacob has been in a nervous spot with Esau coming (Genesis 32:6). But in this fight he doesn't run. He says, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” (Genesis 32:26). The man's word for him is “prevailed” (Genesis 32:28).

I can see it, with a dislocated hip and all. But the man says the opposite: “…and you have prevailed.” (Genesis 32:28). Jacob is hurt, but the man calls it prevailing. Sometimes the limp and the win show up together.

Yes, blessed. The man doesn't give his name, but the text says, “Then he blessed Jacob there.” (Genesis 32:29). That's exactly what Jacob had asked for in verse 26. I think he got what he held on for.
No warning shows up here. After the man asks, “Why do you ask my name?” the text says, “Then he blessed Jacob there.” (Genesis 32:29). No lecture, no scolding. Just a blessing.

Thanks would be a nice touch after a whole night of wrestling. But the text doesn't say that. It says, “Then he blessed Jacob there.” (Genesis 32:29). A blessing is what Jacob asked for (Genesis 32:26).

explanations.answer: He has seen God face to face and his life was spared
explanations.explanation: You got it. Jacob says, “Indeed, I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared.” (Genesis 32:30). That's the reason he gives for the name Peniel. Whatever else happened that night, Jacob names the place for what he says he saw.

explanations.answer: He has won the hardest fight of his whole life
explanations.explanation: That sounds right for a night like this. But Jacob never says it. His reason is, “Indeed, I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared.” (Genesis 32:30). He names the place for what he saw.

explanations.answer: He has finally made peace with his brother Esau
explanations.explanation: Not yet. Esau, Jacob's brother, is still on his way with four hundred men (Genesis 32:6). Jacob's reason for the name is, “Indeed, I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared.” (Genesis 32:30). This passage is about the night, not the meeting.

True, baker. The text says the sun rose above him as he passed by Penuel, and he was limping because of his hip (Genesis 32:31). The man struck that hip during the wrestling (Genesis 32:25). The night left a mark you could see in his walk.

Close, but the text says the opposite. As the sun rose above him, Jacob “was limping because of his hip.” (Genesis 32:31). That's the hip the man struck and dislocated (Genesis 32:25). So Jacob leaves the night with a limp.

explanations.answer: Jacob's hip was struck near that tendon
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. “…the Israelites do not eat the tendon attached to the socket of the hip, because the socket of Jacob's hip was struck near that tendon.” (Genesis 32:32). The night is remembered at the table. It was still true when this was written.

explanations.answer: That tendon was set aside for the priests
explanations.explanation: The text never says anything about priests here. Its reason is, “…because the socket of Jacob's hip was struck near that tendon.” (Genesis 32:32). The habit goes back to Jacob's hip. Nobody is saving that piece for anyone.

explanations.answer: That tendon was used to make bowstrings
explanations.explanation: Bowstrings are a creative guess, but the text doesn't mention them. It says the Israelites do not eat that tendon “…because the socket of Jacob's hip was struck near that tendon.” (Genesis 32:32). The reason is the night at the Jabbok. It's a memory of that wrestling.
